The issue seems serious but the part about Australia and 000 that would ban an attacked device seems the typical LLM-being-too-anal paragraph, and completely lacking common sense.

Maybe I'm wrong and naive but given that the AU law was done to force people move forward from 3G only phones because the network was being shutdown and 000 moved to 5G (I believe), it's a law for operator to contact their customers still using an old phone and migrate them to a newer one. I doubt they will block automatically the number if you are under that DOS for a few days in a row.

As an ex-Google ISE, part of my work was to review security vulnerability reports to us. If this report came on my lap I would definitely have flagged this as a severe security issue. Just a DoS yes, but a severe DoS. I did tier two engineering reviews though. From the website's timeline it seems like a tier one triager dismissed it. And I would see this happen occasionally: tier one triagers either dismissing things that shouldn't, or the reverse, flagging things that don't deserve it. My personal opinion is that the quality of Google's work has declined somewhat in the last decade. Disappointing...

Google has clearly flagged this as "not a security issue", repeatedly. It's a weird bug for sure, but what's the scenario here?

Correct me if I'm wrong, but the carrier configuration messages can normally only come from carriers. The demo APK sends a message to the phone itself, but sending SMS messages requires special confirmation.

Practically speaking, what's the risk?

It is more likely a severe communication issue happened. A related fix was committed by Google on June 15th [0] and was apparently assigned CVE-2026-58882. GrapheneOS [1] was able to ship the fix through the security preview channel as early as July, but it will otherwise be in the upcoming November security bulletin.

  > A single malformed WAP Push SMS crashes com.android.phone on Android, dropping active calls (including emergency calls), with zero interaction from the victim.
An easier way to deliver the point across could be:

  > Anyone can send an specially crafted SMS to repeatedly crash the victim's phone app on Android without user interaction. Google didn't fix it, here's an app you can download to send that SMS and disable anyone's phone remotely.
Just my 2 cents for OP, good job on finding and reporting this and it sounds great that it was actually patched, glad you persisted through the frustration of dealing with google's triaging.
